passage:
Dear Lavanya,

You asked how I finally started walking every day when I had failed all last year. Here is my thinking. I used to say, "I'll walk sometime today," and "sometime" never came. Every day I had to decide when, and by evening I was tired and had no energy for the decision.

So I wrote one sentence on a card: When the toothbrush goes back in the cup each morning, I walk for twenty minutes. No deciding, no bargaining. The teeth part happens anyway, and the walk hangs on it like a coat on a hook.

On a rushed day it might shrink, but the sentence stays. Twelve mornings so far.

Shreya

qa.q: What is the sentence that Shreya wrote on the card?
qa.a: When the toothbrush goes back in the cup each morning, I walk for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling each evening when 'sometime today' never came, and why?
qa.a: Shreya was drained and probably discouraged, since deciding every single day used up the energy by evening.

qa.q: What could Shreya do if a morning is truly rushed, and why?
qa.a: Shreya could still step outside for a few minutes, because keeping the link to brushing teeth protects the habit even when the walk is short.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Lavanya may feel curious and pleased that the question got such a thoughtful answer, and may want to try a card of Lavanya's own.

grounding: The person links a walk to an existing morning routine, so the habit no longer needs a daily decision.

"So, Swati, you want to know how Dhruv, of all people, walks every morning now? Let me tell you.
For a year I said I'd exercise 'when I have time'. Every evening I'd decide, and every evening I'd decide no. Too tired, too late, one more episode.
Then I thought, why am I making this decision every day? What if it's already decided? I looked at what I do every single morning without thinking. Brushing. So the rule became: toothbrush down, shoes on. Out the door, twenty-minute loop round the lake, back.
The first week I kept arguing with myself at the sink. By the third week there was no argument. It's just the next thing, like putting on my watch.
I don't feel superhuman. Some days the walk is slow. But I haven't had to decide once in two months."

qa.q: How long is Dhruv's morning loop?
qa.a: It is a twenty-minute loop round the lake.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel about exercise before the new rule?
qa.a: Dhruv felt tired and kept putting it off, deciding 'no' every evening because it was too late or there was one more episode.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv link to an existing routine?
qa.a: Dhruv could tie a few stretches to making the morning tea, since the same cue-then-action trick removes another daily decision.

qa.q: How might Swati see Dhruv's change?
qa.a: Swati seems surprised that Dhruv of all people now walks every morning, and may want to try linking a habit to Swati's own routine.

grounding: Shows a young professional linking a daily walk to brushing teeth in the morning so the habit no longer needs a daily decision.

I'm Hrithik, and I share a flat with Gautam in Gurugram. For months his running shoes sat by the door, clean.
Then in March I heard him talking to himself while making coffee. "Every day I say I'll run later, and later never comes. What do I already do every day, no matter what?" He looked at the kettle. "This."
From the next morning, the pattern was always the same. Kettle on, shoes on. He'd do a fifteen-minute jog around the colony while the water cooled, then come back and make his coffee.
I asked him once if he ever skipped. He said, "If the kettle goes on, I go. That's it. No thinking." I can't tell if he enjoys it, but the shoes aren't clean any more, and he hasn't missed a weekday since.

qa.q: How long was Gautam's morning jog?
qa.a: It was a fifteen-minute jog around the colony.

qa.q: What was Gautam thinking when he looked at the kettle, and how did he feel?
qa.a: He was frustrated that 'later never comes' and hopeful that tying the run to the kettle would remove the choice.

qa.q: What else could Gautam do on days he wakes up late?
qa.a: He could keep the same cue but do a shorter jog, so the kettle still means 'shoes on' even on rushed mornings.

qa.q: How does the change look to Hrithik?
qa.a: Hrithik notices the shoes are no longer clean and that Gautam hasn't missed a weekday, though Hrithik can't tell if Gautam enjoys it.

grounding: Shows a young professional deciding to jog every time the morning kettle goes on, linking the habit to an existing routine.
